title: Spark Runtime Architecture Quest
subtitle: How PySpark jobs run in production platforms

nodes.label: PySpark Code
nodes.whyItMatters: This is where ETL logic is authored.
nodes.safeSentence: Code says what to do, not usually which machines to use.
nodes.commonTrap: Hard-coding infrastructure assumptions in business logic.

nodes.label: Submission Layer
nodes.definition: Starts the Spark job and passes runtime configuration.
nodes.safeSentence: Submission starts the Spark app and passes runtime settings.
nodes.commonTrap: Treating submission details as optional in production.

nodes.label: spark-submit
nodes.definition: Standard Spark command for launching applications.
nodes.safeSentence: spark-submit is the canonical Spark launcher.
nodes.commonTrap: Assuming platforms remove the need to understand launch configuration.

nodes.label: Orchestrator
nodes.definition: Coordinates schedules, dependencies, retries, parameters, and alerts.
nodes.safeSentence: Orchestrators coordinate jobs; Spark executes data processing.

nodes.label: Driver
nodes.definition: Coordinates the Spark application and schedules tasks.
nodes.safeSentence: Driver plans and dispatches Spark tasks.
nodes.commonTrap: Assuming driver does all heavy data processing.

nodes.label: Executors
nodes.definition: Run tasks on partitions and report status/failures.
nodes.safeSentence: Executors run parallel tasks on partitioned data.

nodes.label: Cluster Manager
nodes.definition: Allocates CPU, memory, and machines for Spark applications.
nodes.whyItMatters: Without resources, Spark cannot run at scale.
nodes.safeSentence: Cluster manager provides resources Spark consumes.
nodes.commonTrap: Thinking Spark itself allocates infrastructure directly.

nodes.label: Hadoop / YARN
nodes.definition: Classic enterprise Spark deployment where YARN allocates resources.
nodes.whyItMatters: Common legacy and enterprise architecture pattern.
nodes.safeSentence: YARN is a common Spark resource manager in Hadoop ecosystems.
nodes.commonTrap: Treating Hadoop and Spark as identical.

nodes.label: Kubernetes
nodes.definition: Runs Spark driver and executors as pods.
nodes.safeSentence: Kubernetes can schedule Spark driver/executor pods.
nodes.commonTrap: Assuming Spark architecture changes fundamentally on K8s.

nodes.label: Databricks
nodes.definition: Managed Spark/lakehouse platform with notebooks, jobs, clusters, Delta, and catalog features.
nodes.whyItMatters: Major production platform for Spark data engineering.
nodes.safeSentence: Databricks is a managed Spark/lakehouse platform.
nodes.commonTrap: Equating platform abstractions with Spark internals.

nodes.label: Amazon EMR
nodes.definition: Managed Hadoop/Spark cluster platform on AWS.
nodes.whyItMatters: Gives managed clusters with infrastructure-level control.
nodes.safeSentence: EMR manages Hadoop/Spark cluster infrastructure on AWS.
nodes.commonTrap: Assuming EMR and Glue have identical operating models.

nodes.label: AWS Glue
nodes.definition: Managed Spark ETL service integrated with S3 and Glue Data Catalog.
nodes.safeSentence: Glue is a managed ETL service that can run Spark jobs.
nodes.commonTrap: Expecting full EMR-style infrastructure controls in Glue.

nodes.label: Storage Layer
nodes.whyItMatters: Compute is useless without durable data storage.
nodes.safeSentence: Spark is compute; storage is where data lives.
nodes.commonTrap: Blending compute-layer assumptions into storage semantics.

nodes.label: Catalog / Metadata
nodes.definition: Tracks table names, schemas, locations, and permissions.
nodes.whyItMatters: Enables reliable table discovery and governance.
nodes.safeSentence: Catalogs define what tables mean and where they live.
nodes.commonTrap: Assuming table names imply physical location without metadata.
